name: DNSP-11
lead: DNSP-11 (dopamine neuron stimulating peptide-11) is an experimental 11-amino-acid peptide that researchers derived from the pro-region of glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF). It was proposed as a smaller, easier-to-deliver alternative to full-length GDNF, which has shown protective effects on dopamine neurons in animal models and in some Parkinson's disease trials but is hard to deliver to the brain because of its size.[1]

It is listed here because neurotrophic peptides appear in longevity and nootropic peptide catalogues, where brain-health claims are sometimes linked to mood, drive and general vitality. Any appearance link would be indirect, through brain and dopamine function rather than through a direct effect on skin, hair or body, and no published work connects DNSP-11 to appearance outcomes.

Published work on DNSP-11 consists of cell-culture and animal studies in rats and rhesus macaques, in which the peptide has been given directly into the brain or repeatedly through the nose.[1][2][3][4] No human clinical trial has been published, and it is not an approved drug.
infobox: Academic neuroscience groups; first described in a 2010 PLoS ONE paper[1]

paras: Glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) supports the survival of dopamine and motor neurons and was the first member of its protein family to be identified, in 1991; a foundational paper by Lin and colleagues appeared in Science in 1993.[6] GDNF is made as a 211-amino-acid precursor (pro-GDNF) that is cleaved by several proteases, including furin, into a 134-amino-acid mature form, and it signals through the RET receptor with GFRA1, activating ERK and PI3K/AKT pathways.[6] The pro-region left behind after cleavage is the part from which DNSP-11 was derived.[1]

Clinical trials of delivering GDNF to the brains of people with Parkinson's disease have produced mixed results. A five-year randomized, double-blind trial begun in 2012 at the University of Bristol enrolled 41 participants, each with a skull port for infusion directly into the brain; the 2019 report in Brain found no statistically significant difference from placebo while confirming effects on damaged brain cells.[6] Delivery is the main obstacle, which motivated work on smaller fragments that might travel more easily.[1][2] A gene-therapy approach, AB-1005 (AAV2-GDNF), entered a phase 1b trial in 2020 and a phase 2 trial, REGENERATE-PD, began recruiting in 2024.[6]

A 2025 review of GDNF isoforms notes that GDNF is not currently used clinically because trials gave conflicting results, and that alternative-splicing products and small isoforms are being studied because they are smaller and show less dose-response dependence.[8]

Outside the brain, GDNF has also been reported to promote hair follicle formation and wound healing by acting on bulge stem cells, and it regulates kidney development and spermatogenesis.[6] These roles belong to the full protein; no study has tested DNSP-11 for hair or skin.

DNSP-11 is an amidated peptide of 11 amino acids. In the 2011 comparison of DNSP-5, DNSP-11 and DNSP-17, the three synthetic peptides were all soluble and stable for a month under varied storage conditions, and differed in whether they bind heparin, as GDNF itself does.[5]

A model of how the human GDNF precursor is processed proposes that cleavage of the pro-region yields smaller amidated peptides with biological activity, including an 11-amino-acid peptide named DNSP-11 [1][4]. In rat studies, a single dose delivered to the substantia nigra altered dopamine neuron function, and cell experiments showed increased ERK 1/2 phosphorylation [4]. A comparison of three synthetic peptides derived from the pro- and mature GDNF sequence evaluated their physical properties and protective activity in vitro [5].

In the 2010 paper, DNSP-11 supported the survival and neurite outgrowth of fetal mesencephalic neurons in culture, protected MN9D cells from 6-hydroxydopamine toxicity with fewer TUNEL-positive cells and lower caspase-3 activity, and, when injected into a normal adult rat substantia nigra, was rapidly taken up by neurons and raised resting dopamine levels.[1] A 2011 study of DNSP-5, DNSP-11 and DNSP-17 found all three soluble and stable for a month under varied storage conditions, found that DNSP-11 and DNSP-5 do not bind heparin (DNSP-17 does, like GDNF), and reported dose-dependent protection of HEK-293 cells from staurosporine and 3-nitropropionate toxicity by DNSP-11.[5]

A 2019 immunohistochemistry study in rat brain found DNSP-11 signal largely co-localised with GDNF at post-natal day 10, but remaining intense in adult animals, including the locus ceruleus where GDNF is not expressed, suggesting a distinct distribution.[7]
No studies found in humans. Research is limited to cell and animal work.

In a rat model, a 2015 study developed a method for repeated intranasal delivery of DNSP-11 in normal rats and in a unilateral model of Parkinson's disease.[2] In a 2018 study, the peptide was delivered intranasally in escalating doses for 10 weeks to awake rhesus macaques without sedation; the authors reported striatal target engagement through dopamine-metabolite changes, no observable adverse behavioural effects or weight loss, and diffuse brain distribution of a radiolabelled dose.[3] A 2014 study delivered a single dose to the rat substantia nigra to examine dopamine neuron function and showed increased ERK 1/2 phosphorylation in cell experiments.[4] These are preclinical studies and do not establish effects in people.

The 2010 study found that DNSP-11 injected into a normal adult rat substantia nigra was rapidly taken up by neurons and raised resting dopamine levels, and the 2018 macaque study of ten weeks of repeated intranasal delivery is the closest preclinical model to human use.[1][3] Mid-sized primate work of this kind is typically a step toward later safety testing; no such human testing of DNSP-11 has been published.

DNSP-11 is not an approved medicine. It is mainly a laboratory research peptide described in academic neuroscience papers, and neurotrophic peptides as a category appear in longevity and nootropic peptide catalogues where brain-health claims are made about mood, drive and vitality.[1][8] Those claims are not tested in humans for DNSP-11.

card.summary: An experimental GDNF-derived brain peptide studied only in rats and monkeys, with no human trials and no appearance data.
card.note: Preclinical only; no human studies found.

quick.overview:
DNSP-11 is an 11-amino-acid peptide derived from a precursor region of GDNF, a protein that supports dopamine neurons. It was developed as a smaller candidate for Parkinson's disease research.

Published studies are in cells, rats and rhesus macaques. No human trials were found, and nothing in the sources links it to appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Researchers propose that processing of the GDNF precursor yields small peptides such as DNSP-11, which in rat experiments changed dopamine neuron function and increased ERK 1/2 signalling in cells.
quick.risks: Its safety in humans has not been studied in published trials. It is not an approved drug, and animal studies do not establish human effects.

chain: Peptide derived from the GDNF pro-region

angle.text: DNSP-11 is a research peptide studied for dopamine neuron protection in Parkinson's disease models. Any link to appearance is hypothetical and runs through brain function; no study has examined looks.
